To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
C transfer from fungus to the orchid occurs after the fungal peloton has been lysed.

we used (13) CO-2 labelling and high-resolution secondary ion imaging to trace C transfers across the interface between the fungal and orchid cells in mycorrhiza formed by an obligate myco-heterotropic orchid (Rhizanthella gardeneri).
C was transferred from the mycorrhzal fungus to the orchid, but that this occurred only after the fungal peloton had lysed.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the fundamental question of how mycorrhizae facilitate nutrient transfer and the mechanisms of this process, and our findings will contribute to our understanding of the role of orchid mycobionts in the C economy of terrestrial ecosystems.
the role of the orchid mycorhiza in facilitating nutrient transfers to an obligately mycoheterotrophic orchids, and how this may influence orchid evolution.
the dynamics of C in mycorrhiza, a symbiosis that has evolved to facilitate the survival of a plant lineage that is dependent on mycorrhizae for all of its C requirements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
C transfer from fungus to orchid occurs only after peloton lysis, but this does not exclude that C transfer from peloton to orchid may occur at the same time.
C transfer occurs after peloton lysis, but it is possible that C transfer occurs across pre-lysed mycorrhizae, and that this may be the dominant pathway of C transfer in other orchids.
C transfers from the fungus to the orchid, and vice versa, but not across intact mycorhrizal interfaces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
C transfer from fungus to orchid in orchid mycorhizas is likely a passive process.
the C transfer in R. gardeneri mycorrhizals likely occurs through the fungal hyphae and not across mycorrhiza interfaces.

orchid myco-heterrotrophy is not a simple case of C transfer across the mycorhizal interface, but that it involves the lysis of fungal pelotons, and the subsequent transfer of C to orchids via the fungal mycelia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the orchid mycorhizal interface is not a site of active C transfer.
the mycorrhiza interface of R. gardeneri is highly impermeable to C transfer.
nanoSIMS can be used to trace C transfers in orchid mycorhizas, but it may not be the best technique for detecting C transfer at mycorrhizae interfaces.
